html:
SMTO-GWT-0049 — SMTO couldn't keep up with a command's output

GUID: f519f2cd-9992-4b08-a8e7-470c385666be
Slug: gateway-observation-overflow
Domain: GWT · Subsystem: gwt

What happened

  • A command running on a Gateway computer sent output faster than SMTO could read it, or sent one very large piece, so SMTO stopped reading. The command itself may still have run, or may still be running.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. In the same conversation, ask SMTO to check what the command changed on that computer, for example whether the expected files exist or the program is still running, without running it again. SMTO lost the command's output, not necessarily the command, so its work may already be done.
  2. If the command is still running, wait for it to finish before starting it again. Two copies of the same command running together could clash or do the work twice.
  3. If the work isn't done, ask SMTO to run the command again but save its output to a file and show you only a short summary or the last lines. Smaller output stays within what SMTO can read at once, so this message doesn't come back.

What success looks like

  • You know whether the command's work is done, and any new run finishes with its output shown in the conversation.

If it still fails

  • Check whether the earlier action already happened before trying it again. Select Copy error details and send them, with the command you ran, to the person who manages that Gateway. Don't rerun a command that changes files or settings until you know what the first run did.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • An outbound Gateway stream exceeded its 64-event observation queue or the 256 KiB per-event limit, so the Server discarded that stream's queued events and ended collection with a 507 error; complete output was not obtained.

What this means

  • An outbound stream produced messages faster than its bounded observation queue could retain them; overflow ended reliable output collection. The retained phase, target and receipt determine what executed. Rendering this definition adds no probe, retries, dispatch or changes to resource ownership.

Why this can happen

  • An outbound stream produced messages faster than its bounded observation queue could retain them; overflow ended reliable output collection.

How to diagnose it

  • Locate the original job and retained log or receipt; distinguish observer overflow from the command's own result.

How to fix it

  • Treat the command's effect as unknown: inspect the target on the Gateway host (files, processes, service or job state) to see what the command did before rerunning anything. For any follow-up, reduce output volume (redirect to a file and read it in parts, filter or paginate) so each stream event stays under 256 KiB and the Server can keep pace.
  • Inspect the existing job or receipt and retrieve retained output through its log controls. Reconcile any uncertain effects before another mutation.

Retry and execution caution

  • Inspect and reconcile authoritative state before repeating a mutation. Do not blindly retry.

How to verify the fix

  • The original execution outcome is reconciled and retained output is inspected with any remaining gap identified.

What not to do

  • Do not repeat a mutation while the earlier outcome or current owner is unresolved.

Technical notes

  • The retained phase, target and receipt determine what executed. Rendering this definition adds no probe, retries, dispatch or changes to resource ownership.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
